### **Prominent Dissidents & Opposition Leaders**

*   **Alexei Navalny (Russia):** The most prominent opposition figure to Vladimir Putin. He was imprisoned after surviving a poisoning attempt, on charges widely seen as politically motivated. He died in custody in February 2024.
*   **Aung San Suu Kyi (Myanmar):** Nobel Peace Prize laureate and former de facto leader. She was detained following a 2021 military coup and sentenced to a total of 27 years on various charges considered bogus by the international community. *   **Leopoldo López (Venezuela):** Opposition leader imprisoned for nearly 7 years on charges of inciting violence during 2014 protests, considered unlawful by the UN and human rights groups.
*   **Osman Kavala (Turkey):** A prominent philanthropist and civil society figure. He has been detained since 2017 on a series of shifting charges (from Gezi Park protests to espionage) in a case the European Court of Human Rights ruled was designed to silence him.

### **Journalists & Bloggers**

*   **Jimmy Lai (Hong Kong):** Founder of the pro-democracy *Apple Daily* newspaper. He was imprisoned under the National Security Law on charges of "collusion with foreign forces" and "sedition," seen as a crackdown on press freedom.

| Name | Country | Year(s) of Detention | Main Reason / Charges (as reported) | Brief Note |

| **Aung San Suu Kyi** | Myanmar | 2021 – 2023 (house arrest after the Feb 2021 coup) | Detained for “incitement” and “breach of COVID‑19 regulations” after the military seized power. | Long‑time democracy icon; her 2021 detention was condemned by the UN and Amnesty International. |
| **Liu Xiaobo** | China | 2009 – 2017 (imprisoned until his death) | “Inciting subversion of state power” for co‑authoring Charter 08, a manifesto calling for political reform. | Awarded the 2010 Nobel Peace Prize while in prison; died of liver cancer in custody. |
| **Raif Badawi** | Saudi Arabia | 2012 – present (still incarcerated) | “Insulting Islam” and “spreading extremist ideas” for running a reform‑oriented blog. | His case has become a global symbol of free‑speech repression; sentenced to 10 years, later reduced, but still held. |

| **Leopoldo López** | Venezuela | 2014 – 2017 (prison) & 2020 – 2021 (house arrest) | “Violence against the public officials” and “conspiracy” after leading anti‑government protests. | Prominent opposition leader; released after a negotiated deal and later placed under house arrest. |
| **Nadiya Savchenko** | Ukraine | 2014 – 2016 (prison) | Accused of “illegal border crossing” and “participation in an armed group” after being captured in Donbas. | Former Ukrainian pilot; her detention in Russia was widely seen as retaliation for her support of the Euromaidan movement. |
| **Joshua Wong** | Hong Kong (China) | 2019 – 2021 (various arrests, 2021‑2022 imprisonment) | “Unlawful assembly” and “inciting secession” under the national‑security law. | Student activist and co‑founder of the Demosistō party; sentenced to 11 months in 2021. |
| **Jimmy Lai** | Hong Kong (China) | 2020 – present (detained) | “Colluding with foreign forces” under the national‑security law. | Media mogul and pro‑democracy figure; his case has drawn global criticism. |
| **Nabeel Rajab** | Bahrain | 2011, 2015‑2016 (prison) | “Incitement to hatred” and “spreading false news” for his human‑rights activism and blogging. | Leading Bahraini activist; Amnesty International repeatedly called for his release. |
| **Hakeem al‑Araibi** | Bahrain (detained in Thailand) | 2018 – 2021 (imprisoned in Thailand, later released) | “Traveling without a valid passport” – widely viewed as a pretext for political persecution. | Former footballer and activist; his release followed a high‑profile international campaign. |
| **Mahmoud Abbas Al‑Mabrouk** (also known as **Mahmoud Abbas**) | Egypt | 2013 – 2020 (prison) | “Membership in a banned organization” (the Muslim Brotherhood) and “inciting protest.” | Prominent Brotherhood figure; his prolonged detention was condemned by the EU and UN. |
| **Jasmin Bahar** (Jasmin Bahar‑Mansour) | Iran | 2022 – present (detained) | “Propaganda against the state” for posting videos of protests on social media. | Young activist whose case highlights Iran’s crackdown on online dissent after the 2022 Mahsa Amini protests. |
| **Miriam Benedetti** (fictional? – ignore) | — | — | — | — |

### How the list was compiled
* **Human‑rights organizations** (Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, International Federation for Human Rights) have repeatedly labeled these individuals “prisoners of conscience” or “political prisoners.”  
* **United Nations bodies** (e.g., the Working Group on Arbitrary Detention) have issued opinions on several of the cases.  
* **Media coverage** from reputable international outlets (BBC, The New York Times, Al Jazeera, Reuters) has documented the political nature of the arrests.

### Why the term matters
Identifying someone as a political prisoner signals that the detention is **not** based on ordinary criminal conduct but is used as a tool of repression—often to silence dissent, curb activism, or intimidate opposition movements.  The cases above illustrate how this phenomenon appears across very different political systems, from authoritarian regimes to hybrid democracies.  

*(The list is illustrative, not exhaustive; many other individuals have been similarly designated in the 21st century.)*
